title: Church of the Holy Trinity v. United States (1892)
shortTitle: Church of the Holy Trinity v. United States (1892) — Katzmann account
summary: A statute's broad words will not be applied to a case that falls within their letter when the statute's purpose, history and title show that the legislature never intended to reach it.
notes:
Key line: It is a familiar rule, that a thing may be within the letter of the statute and yet not within the statute, because not within its spirit, nor within the intention of its makers. (Justice Brewer)

Citation: 143 U.S. 457 (1892).

sections.Parties: The plaintiff in error was the Church of the Holy Trinity, a religious society incorporated under the laws of New York and located in New York City. The defendant in error was the United States, which sued the church to recover the penalty prescribed by the Alien Contract Labor Act of 1885 for assisting an alien to migrate under a contract to perform labor or service. The alien was E. Walpole Warren, a clergyman residing in England whom the church engaged as its rector and pastor. Seaman Miller argued for the church; Assistant Attorney General Maury submitted the Government's case on brief.
sections.Material Facts: In September 1887 the church contracted with Warren, then an alien living in England, to move to New York City and serve as its rector and pastor. Warren came and entered upon that service. The Act of February 26, 1885, 23 Stat. 332, made it unlawful for any person or corporation to prepay transportation or in any way assist or encourage the importation or migration of any alien into the United States under a contract made before migration to perform labor or service of any kind. Section 5 exempted professional actors, artists, lecturers, singers and domestic servants, and skilled workmen in industries not yet established here. The title of the Act described it as one to prohibit the importation and migration of foreigners and aliens under contract or agreement to perform labor. The Government contended that a rector renders service for compensation and that the words of any kind made the prohibition universal outside the listed exceptions.
sections.Procedural History: The United States brought an action in the Circuit Court for the Southern District of New York to recover the statutory penalty. The Circuit Court held that the church's contract with Warren fell within the prohibition of the Act and entered judgment for the Government, 36 Fed. 303. The church took a writ of error to the Supreme Court of the United States. The case was argued and submitted on January 7, 1892, and decided on February 29, 1892. The Court reversed the judgment and remanded for further proceedings. Justice Brewer delivered the opinion for a unanimous Court.
sections.Issue: Does the Act of February 26, 1885, which forbids assisting the migration of any alien under a prior contract to perform labor or service of any kind, apply to a contract between a religious society in the United States and an alien clergyman residing abroad by which he agreed to come to this country and serve as the society's rector and minister? The Court conceded that the contract fell within the letter of the statute, so the question became whether a court may decline to apply the plain words to a case the legislature did not have in mind.
sections.Holding: No. The Act does not apply to the church's contract with its rector. Although the contract is within the letter of the statute, it is not within its spirit or the intention of its makers. The title of the Act, the evil it was passed to remedy, the committee reports in Congress, and the religious character of the American people all show that Congress aimed at the importation of cheap unskilled manual labor and never intended to penalize a church for calling a minister from abroad. The judgment of the Circuit Court is reversed and the case remanded.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Brewer began by admitting the force of the Government's textual argument: a rector's relation to his church is one of service, the statute reaches service of any kind, and the specific exemptions for actors, singers and domestic servants suggest that everything else was covered. He then stated the familiar rule that a thing may be within the letter of a statute and yet not within the statute because not within its spirit or its makers' intention, and cited cases rejecting literal readings that produced absurd results. Reading the statute as a whole, he found three guides to intent. First, the title spoke only of labor, which in common speech means manual labor. Second, the evil Congress addressed was the practice of large employers importing ignorant and servile laborers under contract to depress wages; the Senate committee report stated that the bill would have been limited to manual labor had time permitted amendment and that no such construction was needed because the courts would so read it. Third, no purpose of action against religion could be imputed to any legislation of this country, which Brewer supported with a long review of colonial charters, state constitutions and judicial statements calling this a Christian nation. Because the whole history and life of the country showed the transaction could not have been legislated against intentionally, the court's duty was to hold it outside the statute despite the breadth of its words.
